item.title: Building an ESP32 Self-Levelling Gimbal: From Simulation to a Custom PCB
item.content:encoded:
My experience designing a two-axis stabilisation system using an ESP32, an MPU6050, PID control and a 3D-printed frame.

I’ve been wanting to get more experience with electronics and embedded systems, particularly projects where I could combine them with what I’ve been learning in mechanical engineering.

One project I decided to take on was a self-levelling gimbal. The idea was fairly simple, build a platform that can detect when it’s tilted and automatically correct itself using two servo motors.

I wanted to go further than just getting a circuit working on a breadboard. My plan was to write the firmware, design my own PCB, modify a mechanical frame in Fusion 360, 3D print the parts and put everything together into a working prototype.

It ended up being a really useful project, although I ran into quite a few issues along the way, particularly with the power supply and mechanical design.

1. How the Gimbal Works

The gimbal operates on two axes: roll and pitch. When the platform tilts, the system measures the change in orientation and commands the servos to bring it back towards its target position.

For the controller, I used an ESP32, with an MPU6050 inertial measurement unit (IMU) to measure acceleration and angular velocity.

One issue with using an IMU is that neither sensor gives a perfect angle measurement on its own.

The accelerometer can estimate tilt using gravity, but its readings can be affected by movement and vibration. The gyroscope responds much faster, but integrating angular velocity introduces drift over time.

To deal with this, I used a complementary filter that combines both measurements.

The filter coefficient was set to 0.96, giving more weight to the integrated gyroscope reading while gradually correcting drift using the accelerometer.

Once the angle is estimated, the ESP32 compares it with the target and calculates how much each servo needs to move.

I implemented separate PID controllers for roll and pitch.

After tuning the physical prototype, I settled on the following controller gains for both roll and pitch:

  • Proportional gain (Kp): 1.5
  • Integral gain (Ki): 0.0
  • Derivative gain (Kd): 0.1

I ended up leaving the integral gain at zero, meaning the final controller was effectively operating as a PD controller. For the limited range of movement I was working with, I didn’t find integral control necessary.

2. Starting With Simulation

Before buying components or putting anything together, I started in Wokwi.

I used it to simulate the ESP32, MPU6050, servo motors and an OLED display. This allowed me to work on the basic firmware and check how the different components communicated without needing the physical hardware.

I also worked on a web dashboard that the ESP32 could host over Wi-Fi.

The dashboard displays the measured roll and pitch angles and allows the user to switch between stabilisation and manual setpoint control.

I added a heartbeat system as well. If the browser stops communicating while the gimbal is in setpoint mode, the ESP32 automatically returns to stabilisation mode.

Simulation was useful for checking the logic, but I knew it wouldn’t tell me everything about how the real servos and mechanical structure would behave.

That became pretty obvious once I started testing the actual hardware.

3. Moving to Physical Hardware

Once I was happy with the basic code, I moved everything onto a breadboard.

This was where I could start checking things properly, such as the servo directions, IMU measurements, power connections and how the controller responded when I moved the sensor.

One decision I made early was to keep the servo power separate from the ESP32.

The MG996R servos can draw quite a lot of current, especially when moving under load. Powering them directly from the ESP32 would have been a poor choice.

Instead, I used an external 5 V supply for the servos, while the ESP32 was powered through USB. Both supplies shared a common ground so that the control signals had the same reference.

After testing the circuit, I wanted to replace the breadboard wiring with something more permanent.

This was also a good opportunity to get more experience with PCB design.

4. Designing My First Gimbal PCB

I used KiCad to design a custom carrier PCB for the ESP32 and the other electronics.

I didn’t need to design an entire ESP32 development board from scratch. The goal was to make a board that could hold the ESP32, connect the servos and MPU6050, and distribute power without having wires running everywhere.

The finished PCB measured 70 × 55 mm and used two copper layers.

I included connectors for both servos, a four-pin connector for the MPU6050, external power input, decoupling capacitors and mounting holes.

I also used socket headers for the ESP32 so that I could remove or replace it without desoldering anything.

After finishing the schematic and routing the board, I ran KiCad’s design-rule checks and prepared the fabrication files.

The PCBs were manufactured with support from PCBWay, who also helped with the 3D-printed parts.

Seeing a design I’d made in KiCad turn into a physical PCB was one of my favourite parts of the project.

There is quite a difference between connecting modules with jumper wires and having to think about connector positions, trace widths, mounting holes and how everything will actually fit inside an enclosure.

5. Designing the Mechanical Frame

For the mechanical design, I started with the self-stabilising platform from HowToMechatronics and modified it in Fusion 360.

The original design included a yaw axis, which I didn’t need, so I removed it and focused on roll and pitch.

I also designed my own electronics enclosure to house the PCB, battery holder, boost converter and wiring.

The enclosure needed enough space for the components while still allowing access to the ESP32’s USB port and the power switch.

I added mounting holes for the PCB and designed a removable lid so I could access the electronics without taking the entire assembly apart.

The parts were FDM printed using PLA at 60% infill.

Once I assembled the frame, I noticed some flexibility in the printed parts, along with small alignment errors.

The platform didn’t sit perfectly level at the servos’ default neutral positions, so I introduced separate neutral offsets in the firmware.

That helped correct the resting position, although it didn’t solve the actual mechanical flex.

6. The Biggest Problem: Power

This was probably the most frustrating part of the project.

The servos worked, the ESP32 could read the MPU6050, and the controller was producing corrective movements. However, once I started asking for larger or more sudden movements, the system became unstable.

My power setup used parallel 18650 cells connected to an MT3608 boost converter, which supplied the 5 V servo rail.

I also included a 1000 µF capacitor to help with short power disturbances.

Even with this setup, the servos weren’t behaving reliably during more aggressive movements.

My main suspicion was that the power supply couldn’t consistently handle the current demanded by the servos. However, I didn’t have measurements of the voltage dips or current spikes, so I couldn’t confirm exactly how much of the problem came from the power supply.

The flexibility of the frame and the mechanical alignment were additional complications.

I spent time adjusting the controller gains, but eventually it became clear that tuning the software alone wasn’t going to solve everything.

For the final demonstration, I restricted each servo to approximately ±5° around its calibrated neutral position.

This gave me a smaller operating range in which I could demonstrate corrective movement without the same level of instability.

It wasn’t the full range of movement I’d originally hoped for, but it allowed me to finish the prototype and identify what needed improving.

7. The Final Result

The completed gimbal could measure the platform’s roll and pitch and command corrective movements through both servos.

I also got the Wi-Fi dashboard working, which displayed live angle readings and allowed me to change the target position from a browser.

The important limitation is that the ±5° figure describes the servo command range, not the accuracy of the stabilisation.

I also didn’t collect proper response measurements such as settling time, overshoot or steady-state error, so I wouldn’t describe the system as a precision stabiliser.

It was a working proof of concept, with enough functionality to demonstrate the feedback system, electronics and mechanical integration.

Demonstration: Watch the Finished Prototype

8. What I’d Do Differently

If I were to rebuild the gimbal, there are a few things I’d change.

The first would be the power supply. I’d use a regulator better suited to the current requirements of the two MG996R servos and measure the supply voltage during operation rather than relying on assumptions.

I’d also redesign parts of the frame to improve rigidity and reduce unwanted movement.

Another improvement would be to log the actual platform angle and servo commands over time. This would let me plot the response to a disturbance and properly investigate settling time, overshoot and controller performance.

That would make PID tuning much more useful because I could compare actual measurements instead of judging the response mainly by eye.

Final Thoughts

Looking back, I think I learned more from the problems with this project than I would have if everything had worked straight away.

I originally thought the main challenge would be writing and tuning the controller. In reality, getting the electronics, power supply, PCB and mechanical structure to work together was just as important.

It also gave me experience taking a project through several stages, from simulation and breadboard testing to PCB design, manufacturing and final assembly.

There are definitely things I’d improve, and I might revisit the gimbal in the future to see how much better I can get it working.

For now, I’m happy that I managed to bring all these different parts together into a physical system, and I’ve got a much better understanding of what I need to consider for my next embedded hardware project.

Project Links

GitHub: ESP32 Self-Levelling Gimbal

Portfolio: Full Engineering Case Study

Demonstration: Watch the Finished Prototype

Acknowledgements: PCB fabrication and 3D printing were supported by PCBWay through its student/non-profit sponsorship programme. The original mechanical design was based on the HowToMechatronics self-stabilising platform, which I modified for this project.

item.title: A Billion Records, One Database Query: When Should You Use a Bloom Filter?
item.content:encoded:
Imagine running an e-commerce platform with one billion product records. Every time a customer opens a product page, adds an item to their basket or checks a product link, your application may need to verify that the product exists.

One query sounds harmless. A thousand queries a second might still be manageable. But what happens when thousands of customers, background jobs and other services all start making these requests simultaneously?

The answer depends on how the database searches for records, how much traffic it receives and how efficiently it uses its resources.

A Bloom filter offers an interesting way to reduce unnecessary database queries. Before exploring it, however, we need to understand why checking a record can become expensive in the first place.

1. Does a billion records make every query slow?

Not necessarily.

Consider a library containing one billion books. If every book is arranged in an unsorted pile, finding a particular title could require checking book after book. If the title is not there, you might have to inspect the entire pile before reaching that conclusion.

Now imagine the same library has a well-maintained catalogue. Instead of examining every book, you follow the catalogue to the relevant shelf and locate the title.

Databases work in a similar way.

The number of records matters, but the database’s access path often matters more.

Case 1: Searching without an index

Suppose we have a products table:

SELECT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM products
    WHERE product_id = 987654321
);

If there is no suitable index, the database may need to scan the table to determine whether the product exists.

The time complexity is typically O(n) in the worst case, where n represents the number of records.

For one billion records, this can mean examining an enormous amount of data. An absent product can be particularly expensive to check because the database cannot stop at a matching row.

The actual cost depends on the execution plan, storage layout and whether data is already in memory.

Case 2: Searching with an index

A suitable index changes the situation considerably.

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_products_product_id
ON products(product_id);

The database can use the index to navigate towards the requested identifier rather than examining every row.

For a B-tree index, the typical search complexity is O(log n). A billion entries correspond to roughly 30 binary-search levels, although a real database index is a multi-level structure with many entries per page.

This does not mean that every lookup requires 30 disk reads. Database pages, caching, index fan-out and storage behaviour determine the actual cost.

An indexed existence query can therefore be very efficient, even with a billion records.

So why would we need anything else?

Because an efficient query can still become expensive when executed at an enormous scale.

2. The real problem: Query volume

Suppose an online shopping platform receives 10,000 product-existence checks every second.

That amounts to:

  • 600,000 checks per minute.
  • 36 million checks per hour.
  • 864 million checks per day.

These numbers assume a constant request rate, but they illustrate how quickly ordinary operations accumulate.

Even if an indexed lookup is inexpensive, the database must still process every request. It needs to manage connections, execute queries, traverse indexes, access relevant pages and return results.

Now imagine that a significant proportion of requests concern product IDs that do not exist. These could come from stale links, bots, invalid client requests or repeated attempts to access removed products.

The database is spending resources proving the absence of something.

That is where the design becomes interesting.

3. What happens when the database is under pressure?

A database does not suddenly fail just because it contains a billion records. Problems usually emerge when the workload approaches or exceeds available capacity.

CPU consumption

Every query requires some processing. With enough concurrent requests, query execution and associated database operations can consume a substantial share of CPU capacity.

Full table scans are particularly costly because they process many more rows than a targeted index lookup.

Disk I/O

An index lookup may require reading index pages and, depending on the query and storage engine, other relevant pages.

If those pages are already in memory, the operation may avoid physical disk access. If not, storage latency becomes important.

Repeated scans can generate much more I/O than targeted lookups.

Connection-pool exhaustion

Applications commonly use a finite database connection pool. When requests arrive faster than connections can complete their work, requests begin waiting.

The result is a queue: users experience higher latency even if the database is still technically available.

Latency under concurrency

A query that normally takes a few milliseconds can take considerably longer when CPU, I/O or connection capacity is saturated.

This is one reason average query latency alone can be misleading. The 95th or 99th percentile latency may reveal problems that the average conceals.

A simple illustration

Assume a database can sustain 8,000 relevant queries per second under a particular workload, while the application sends 10,000 queries per second.

The incoming workload exceeds the measured capacity by 2,000 queries per second. Unless the system sheds load, scales or reduces demand, waiting requests can accumulate.

The figure is illustrative, not a universal database limit. Actual capacity must be established through workload testing.

The important point is that the cost of a query depends on both its individual execution cost and the number of times it must be executed.

4. Introducing the Bloom filter

A Bloom filter is a space-efficient probabilistic data structure that answers a simple question:

Could this element be in the set?

It does not store the complete records. Instead, it maintains a bit array and uses multiple hash functions to represent the identifiers inserted into it.

Think of a nightclub with a guest list.

Instead of looking up every name in the full guest register, a doorman consults a quick screening system.

If the screening system confirms that a name cannot be on the list, the doorman can reject it without opening the register. If the screening system says the name might be present, the doorman checks the actual register.

A Bloom filter works along those lines, with one important distinction: it can occasionally say that an identifier might exist when it does not.

How it works

Suppose we insert three product identifiers:

P101
P205
P310

Each identifier is processed by several hash functions. Each function identifies a position in a bit array, and those positions are set to 1.

When a request arrives for P999, the filter calculates the corresponding positions.

If even one required bit is 0, the identifier was definitely not inserted into the filter. The database lookup can be skipped.

If every required bit is 1, the identifier might exist. The application must query the database to confirm.

The filter does not tell us which products exist, nor does it retrieve product information. Its job is simply to eliminate certain unnecessary lookups.

5. How much work can a Bloom filter save?

Return to our platform receiving 10,000 existence checks per second.

Suppose 90% of those requests concern identifiers absent from the database. Assume the Bloom filter is correctly maintained and has no false negatives, and that the remaining 10% require one database query each.

Without the filter, the database receives 10,000 queries per second.

With the filter, the 9,000 definitely absent identifiers can be rejected before reaching the database. The remaining requests proceed to verification.

Metric                          | Without Bloom filter | With Bloom filter
--------------------------------|----------------------|-------------------
Incoming checks per second      | 10,000               | 10,000
Checks rejected before database | 0                    | 9,000
Database queries per second     | 10,000               | 1,000
Reduction in database queries   | —                    | 90%

These are illustrative figures. They assume the stated proportion of absent IDs and exclude false positives for simplicity.

A Bloom filter can also produce false positives, meaning that some absent identifiers pass through to the database. Consequently, the actual reduction may be lower.

Still, when nonexistent IDs are common, avoiding even a large proportion of database queries can make a meaningful difference.

6. What is the time complexity?

The complexity of each operation helps explain why Bloom filters are attractive.

Operation                       | Typical time complexity | Explanation
--------------------------------|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------
Full table scan                 | O(n)                    | May examine all records
B-tree index lookup             | O(log n)                | Navigates a multi-level index
Hash-table lookup               | Expected O(1)           | Depends on the hash table and its load
Bloom filter insertion          | O(k)                    | Computes k hash positions
Bloom filter membership check   | O(k)                    | Checks k bit positions

Here, n is the number of database records and k is the number of hash functions used by the Bloom filter.

When k is fixed, Bloom filter insertion and membership checks are O(1) with respect to the number of stored elements.

There is a qualification worth remembering: constant-time membership testing does not guarantee that a Bloom filter is faster than an indexed database query. It is an additional screening operation, and its value depends on the workload.

7. Build a demonstrable small Bloom Filter

Let’s build a Bloom filter using just 3 product IDs and an array of 10 bits. We’ll walk through every bit so you can see exactly how it works.

Step 1: Start with an empty bit array

Imagine your database contains these products:

  • P10
  • P20
  • P30

Our Bloom filter has 10 bits, numbered from 0 to 9. Initially, every bit is 0.

Step 2: Insert product P10

For this example, we’ll use two simple hash functions. They are deliberately chosen for easy arithmetic, not for production use.

  • Hash function 1: take the number after P and calculate number % 10.
  • Hash function 2: calculate (number + 3) % 10.

For P10:

  • Hash 1: 10 % 10 = 0
  • Hash 2: (10 + 3) % 10 = 3

So we switch bits at positions 0 and 3 from 0 to 1.

Notice that the Bloom filter does not store P10 itself. It only marks two positions in the array.

Step 3: Insert product P20

Apply the same hash functions:

  • Hash 1: 20 % 10 = 0
  • Hash 2: (20 + 3) % 10 = 3

Both positions are already 1.

Nothing changes in the array. That is perfectly fine: multiple product IDs can map to the same bits.

Step 4: Insert product P30

Calculate its positions:

  • Hash 1: 30 % 10 = 0
  • Hash 2: (30 + 3) % 10 = 3

Again, both bits are already 1.

Our final array is still:

This is a very small filter, so collisions are easy to create.

Step 5: Check whether P40 exists

Now suppose a request arrives for P40, which we never inserted.

Calculate its hash positions:

  • Hash 1: 40 % 10 = 0
  • Hash 2: (40 + 3) % 10 = 3

Check the array:

Bit position | Current bit | Result
-------------|-------------|-------
0            | 1           | Pass
3            | 1           | Pass

Both bits are 1, so the Bloom filter says P40 might exist.

But P40 was never inserted! This is a false positive. The application must query the database, which will return that the ID does not exist.

Why did this happen? Because P10, P20 and P30 had already switched on the same bits.

Step 6: Check whether P41 exists

Now check P41:

  • Hash 1: 41 % 10 = 1
  • Hash 2: (41 + 3) % 10 = 4

Look at the array:

Bit position | Current bit | Result
-------------|-------------|-------
1            | 0           | Fail
4            | 0           | Fail

At least one bit is 0, so P41 is definitely absent from the filter.

The application can reject this ID without querying the database, assuming the filter has been correctly maintained.

Product ID | Inserted into filter? | Bits checked | Bloom filter result             | Database query needed?
-----------|----------------------|--------------|----------------------------------|-----------------------
P10        | Yes                  | 0, 3         | Might exist                      | For confirmation, yes
P20        | Yes                  | 0, 3         | Might exist                      | For confirmation, yes
P30        | Yes                  | 0, 3         | Might exist                      | For confirmation, yes
P40        | No                   | 0, 3         | Might exist (false positive)     | Yes
P41        | No                   | 1, 4         | Definitely absent                | No

The two hash functions above are intentionally simplistic and cause every inserted example to collide. Real Bloom filters use better-distributed hash functions and appropriately sized arrays to make false positives much less likely.

The central idea: A Bloom filter remembers which bit positions have been switched on, not which IDs switched them on. If any required bit is off, an ID was not inserted. If all required bits are on, the ID might have been inserted or those bits might belong to other IDs.

8. How much memory does it need?

Bloom filters are particularly useful because they represent a large set using relatively little memory.

For example, a filter designed for one million elements and a 1% false-positive probability needs approximately 9.6 million bits, or about 1.14 MiB, before implementation overhead.

The approximate false-positive probability is:

Where:

  • p is the false-positive probability.
  • n is the expected number of inserted elements.
  • m is the number of bits in the array.
  • k is the number of hash functions.

For a fixed target false-positive rate, memory requirements grow approximately linearly with the number of elements.

A filter designed for one million identifiers cannot simply be assumed to perform equally well for one billion. Its capacity and error rate must be planned for the expected number of inserted identifiers.

9. Where should the Bloom filter live?

For an application, the filter might be maintained in application memory or as part of a storage engine.

An application-level implementation could look like this:

def product_exists(product_id):
    if not bloom_filter.might_contain(product_id):
        return False
    return database.exists(product_id)

The example assumes a suitable Bloom filter library and database client are configured.

If the filter says the ID is absent, the function returns immediately. Otherwise, the database remains the authority.

For a distributed application, however, there are additional considerations:

  • Initial population: The filter must be built from the correct set of identifiers.
  • New records: Insertions must update the filter reliably.
  • Deleted records: Standard Bloom filters cannot safely delete individual elements. A deleted product may continue to appear potentially present, causing an unnecessary database query.
  • Multiple application instances: Each instance needs a consistent filter or a deliberate strategy for sharing updates.
  • Capacity planning: A filter that becomes saturated produces more false positives, reducing its usefulness.

One especially important detail is update consistency. If a newly created product is missing from the filter, the filter might incorrectly reject a valid ID. A robust design must ensure that its negative answers are safe, even when records are being created or updated.

10. When is a Bloom filter worth using?

A Bloom filter is worth considering when:

  • The system receives many requests for nonexistent identifiers.
  • Database capacity is constrained by unnecessary lookups.
  • The identifier set is large enough that a compact in-memory representation is attractive.
  • A small false-positive probability is acceptable.
  • The team can maintain the filter correctly as the underlying data changes.

It may not be worthwhile when nearly every requested identifier exists, indexed queries are already inexpensive, or filter maintenance introduces more complexity than the saved database work justifies.

There are also other possible optimisations, including application-level caching, rate limiting, request validation and database read replicas. Each addresses a different aspect of the workload.

Conclusion

A billion records is not, by itself, a reason to introduce a Bloom filter. A well-indexed database can handle large datasets efficiently.

The more useful question is whether the application is repeatedly asking the database to verify identifiers that are not there.

If it is, a Bloom filter can act as a lightweight screening layer. It rejects definite misses quickly, allows possible matches through for verification and reduces the number of requests reaching the database.

The database still does the authoritative work. The Bloom filter simply helps ensure that it does not have to do unnecessary work quite so often.

A Billion Records, One Database Query: When Should You Use a Bloom Filter? was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Claude Code Just Got Mods
item.content:encoded:
I Built 3 That Fix the Problems Every User Hits Daily

Claude Code Mods

Claude Code just shipped a feature that changes who it’s for: mods. Until now, Claude Code was built for people who love the terminal. You typed, it scrolled, and you learned to live with whatever it put on screen. Mods change that. For the first time, you decide what Claude Code shows you, and even what it does.

I use Claude Code every day, and three things bugged me every single day:

  1. “Why did I just hit my limit?” Mid-task, out of nowhere, with a two-hour reset.
  2. “Is it stuck, or almost done?” A wall of tool output scrolling faster than I could read.
  3. “What was that command again?” Slash commands I knew existed and could never remember.

So when mods landed, I built one for each. Here’s the result: same Claude Code, same prompt, same project.

On the left, you wait and hope. On the right, you glance and know: what Claude is doing, how much is left, and when you’ll hit your limit.

  • “Why did I just hit my limit?” → limits-meter: a fuel gauge above your prompt that warns you before you run out.
  • “Is it stuck, or almost done?” → plain-view: one progress card instead of a wall of text.
  • “What was that command again?” → launchpad: your commands as one-click buttons.

All three are free, open source, and install with one line. First, the 60-second version of what a mod is.

Prefer video? The before-and-after runs live in this one:

How does Mods work ?

Think of the widgets on your phone. Same phone, but your home screen shows the weather, your battery, your next meeting. You picked them.

Mods do that for Claude Code. Same Claude Code, with the widgets you pick: a band above your prompt, a panel, a button, a pop-up toast.

And a mod goes one step further than a widget: it can change what Claude Code does, not just what it shows.

Under the hood

Skip this if you don’t write code. Nothing below depends on it.

Claude Code runs on events. Every step fires one: when it draws something on screen, when it runs a tool, when you send a message. A mod registers handlers for those events, and the handlers run as a middleware chain. Each one can watch the event, change it, or replace it with its own output.

If you’ve written a Servlet Filter or a Spring HandlerInterceptor, you already know this shape. A handler that draws on a shared spot calls next(e) and stacks its own row on top of what came back, never in its place. That's why three mods can share the line above your prompt without one erasing the others.

Now, the three problems, and how each mod kills one.

Problem 1: “Why did I just hit my limit?”

Every Claude Code user has been here. You’re mid-task, the session is going well, and then: limit reached. Reset in two hours. Was it the big refactor? The switch to a bigger model? The 40-file search? You have no idea, because nothing warned you.

The workaround is typing /usage after every prompt. Nobody keeps that up.

The fix: limits-meter

limits-meter is a fuel gauge, right above your prompt. It shows, all the time:

  • which model you’re on, and at what effort
  • how much of your 5-hour and weekly limits you’ve used, and when each resets
  • how full Claude’s memory of this conversation (the context window) is

And it looks ahead. At your current pace, will you run out before the reset? It tells you now, not when it’s too late.

It also catches the two moments that burn limits fastest:

  • The conversation gets too full. At 85% of context, a compact button appears. It doesn't compact anything on its own. It types /compact [focus] into your prompt and waits for you.
  • You switch to a bigger model (or to max effort) with the 5-hour window already at 70% or more. One toast tells you how many minutes you have left at your recent pace.
/limits          open the pane: plan windows, context, the last 20 turns
/limits warn N   warn on a costly switch from N% of the 5-hour window (default 70)
/limits hide     hide the band

The payoff: I stopped typing /usage, and this mod has saved me from blowing through my tokens more than once.

Problem 2: “Is it stuck, or almost done?”

You send a request. Claude Code starts working, and the screen fills: every file it reads, every search it runs, every tool call, line after line. It’s all technically useful, and almost none of it answers the only question you have: how far along is it?

Is it almost done? Is it stuck? Did it break something? You scroll, squint, and wait.

The fix: plain-view

plain-view replaces the wall of text with one card above the prompt: your request as a title, Steps 2 of 4, and a progress bar for each task. When the turn ends, the card turns green with how long it took and which files changed.

The part I’m proudest of is what it refuses to hide. If something fails, if Claude needs your permission, if it asks you a question, that always shows, in full. A calm screen that hides a permission dialog would be worse than a noisy one.

plain-view is off until you turn it on: /plain-view on.

Make it yours: what you can configure

Type /plain-view and a settings pane opens with three tabs. Every option is one click, applies to every session, and is saved in /config → plain-view. A [ defaults ] button puts everything back.

Transcript tab: how quiet the screen gets.

  • On: yes hides the tool rows and shows the plan in a card above the prompt; no gives you the usual transcript.
  • The agent’s words: final (default) hides what Claude writes before calling tools and keeps the final answer. none hides all of its words, only the card stays. card moves the answer's first sentence into the card. all shows everything.
  • Ask for a task list: to show real steps, plain-view adds one line to Claude’s system prompt asking it to keep a task list for work of more than two steps. It costs a few tokens per request, and the pane says so. Set it to no and the card reads only the list Claude keeps on its own.

Card tab: what the card looks like.

  • Request on the card: how much of a long request shows as the card’s title. line (default) shows the first line plus a count like +5 lines; joined puts all lines in one, cut at the card's width; auto uses the first line of prose; all shows up to 10 lines under the title.
  • Bar colors: eight palettes, claude, clean, sunset, aurora, ocean, neon, forest and calm (grey, with green only at the end, for the minimalists).
  • Animation: yes runs a shine along the bars while the agent works; no keeps them still, in your theme's colors.

A live preview at the bottom shows a demo card with your choices, so you see the palette before you commit.

General tab: language and icons.

  • Language: auto follows your system's LANG, or force pt-BR or en.
  • Icons: steps as emoji (✅ 🟠 ⚪) or as symbols (✓ ● ○) for terminals that draw emoji at odd widths. auto picks symbols in a JetBrains terminal and emoji elsewhere.

The payoff: I glance at the card and know where Claude is. I only read the transcript when something actually needs me.

Problem 3: “What was that command again?”

Claude Code runs on slash commands. /compact, /context, /resume, /model, /effort, plus every skill and agent you've installed. You know the command exists. You just can't remember what it's called, so you don't use it.

The fix: launchpad

launchpad turns your commands into up to eight one-click buttons. They show when a session starts and after /clear. One click: tidy the conversation, see your limits, pick up yesterday's chat. And any command, skill or agent you have installed can become a button.

Below the prompt sits ◆ pad, a button that opens a control panel with three sections:

  • Controls: the model and the effort level (how hard Claude thinks) as buttons, the current ones marked ●. One press runs /model or /effort for you.
  • Mods: a button for each mod of the collection you have installed, which opens its pane. plain-view also gets its on/off switch here. Mods you don’t have show up as install … buttons.
  • Shortcuts: your launchpad buttons, one click away from any point in the session.

This is where the three mods click together. See limits opens limits-meter. plain-view’s on/off switch lives in the panel. And if a mod is missing, its button doesn’t install anything. It types the install command into your prompt, and waits for your Enter.

Make it yours: what you can configure

Which buttons. /pad configuration opens a pane with your buttons, each with ↑, ↓ and remove, and below them every installed command, skill and agent not yet in the menu, with a filter to type into. Prefer typing? Add one directly, with an optional icon:

/pad add 🔎 Review | /code-review     a button that runs a command or skill
/pad add Reviewer | @reviewer          a button that calls an agent
/pad remove 3                          drop button 3
/pad reset                             back to the default buttons

How a button behaves. /compact runs right away. A command with a blank, like /code-review [level], goes into your prompt with the blank marked, for you to fill in and send. An @agent button puts the request in the prompt and waits for you to say what the task is.

Where the menu lives. /pad place header (the default card under the header), prompt (a row that stays right above the prompt box) or pane (a tab of its own). /pad off hides the menu, /pad on brings it back; ◆ pad stays either way.

Buttons for the whole team. A project can ship its own buttons in .claude/launchpad.json, so everyone who opens the repo gets them:

{
  "buttons": [
    { "icon": "🧾", "label": "Monthly close", "text": "/monthly-close" },
    { "icon": "chart", "label": "Reviewer", "text": "@reviewer" }
  ]
}

Because that text comes from the repository, a project button never runs on its own: a press only puts the command in your prompt, and you read it before pressing Enter.

Language and icons. Like plain-view, it follows your system’s language (pt-BR or en) and switches to symbols instead of emoji in terminals that draw emoji at odd widths. Both live in /config → launchpad.

The payoff: the commands I used to forget are now the ones I use most.

Before you install any mod (mine included)

One thing about mods deserves thirty seconds of your attention.

Before an app reads your photos, your phone asks: “Allow access?” A mod doesn’t ask. It runs inside Claude Code with the same access you have: your files, your settings, the internet. No popup.

So before installing any mod, run three checks:

  1. Does it act on its own? Do the buttons that matter wait for your Enter? Red flag: a button that runs commands, installs or edits without asking.
  2. Does it say what it touches? Is there a “what it reaches” list, and does claude plugin validate agree? Red flag: no list, or network access a status bar doesn't need.
  3. Is it checked? Is the code public, with automated tests? Red flag: closed source, no tests.

Here’s how my three answer them:

  1. Everything starts with your click. The big moves (tidying the conversation, installing a mod) type the command into your prompt and wait. You press Enter, not the mod.
  2. They come with a table. None of the three goes on the internet, runs programs, uses AI on its own, or sends your data anywhere. limits-meter and plain-view don’t even open a file.
  3. 324 automated tests run on every change before it reaches you, and the code is open source.
Not technical? Ask Claude Code to read the mod and tell you what it touches. Or run one command, and it lists every event the mod hooks into and every call it makes:
claude plugin validate ./limits-meter

Install all three (one line each)

All three are free, MIT-licensed, and live in one repo: github.com/ice-lfernandes/claude-code-mods. In a Claude Code session:

/plugin install limits-meter --marketplace ice-lfernandes/claude-code-mods
/plugin install plain-view --marketplace ice-lfernandes/claude-code-mods
/plugin install launchpad --marketplace ice-lfernandes/claude-code-mods

Answer y to add the marketplace, pick a scope, and for plain-view run /plain-view on. Want to try one for a single session first? Clone the repo and run claude --plugin-dir ./limits-meter.

The repo has three more if you want to go further: agent-watch (what each subagent is doing, and a toast when one stalls), test-hud (passing tests in the status line, a toast when the suite turns green), and allowlist-coach (offers to stop asking about a permission you’ve approved five times, and asks before it writes).

Got a different daily annoyance? Build your own

Mods are new, which means most of the useful ones haven’t been built yet. If none of these fixes your daily annoyance, describe the mod you want to Claude Code. It’ll build it for you.

Just give it the same three checks. Especially your own.

Watch the video: I Fixed Claude Code’s Most Annoying Parts With 3 Free Mods More on YouTube: subscribe to Java Plus AI for the full series.

If this made your Claude Code a little calmer, leave a few 👏 (you can clap up to 50 times), and send it to the teammate who still types /usage after every prompt.

Claude Code Just Got Mods was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: AI Agents for a KMP Developer
item.content:encoded:
In my previous article, AI Extensions for a KMP Developer, I gave the same model the same task while gradually extending its capabilities: first with Rules, then with a specialized Skill, and finally with access to official repositories through MCP. Each extension improved the result, but in every run a single agent worked in a single session, trying to keep Gradle, Xcode, and npm in mind at the same time.

This time I decided to take the next step and replace the single agent with a team. Kotlin Multiplatform is particularly well suited for this. The shared logic in KMP is written once, but it has to be integrated into four platform-specific applications, each with its own toolchain, build commands, and error formats. This structure itself suggests how to split the work: one agent per platform and an orchestrator that propagates changes to the shared code.

As an example, I used the five projects from my article KMP: Integrating into Native Projects: the shared module and four applications for Android, iOS, Desktop, and Web. Everything is built from standard Claude Code features: subagents, Skills, hooks, and CLAUDE.md. The main point I want to show is that agents do not become reliable on their own. They work reliably only when trustworthy verification is in place before they start, and when they operate within restrictions enforced by code rather than by the prompt.

Why a Team Instead of a Single Agent

The first idea that comes to mind with several agents is to split them by layers: one writes the domain logic, another the UI, a third the tests. In KMP this split is not very useful. The main difficulty here is not the amount of code, but the fact that each platform lives in its own environment: Xcode and Swift Package Manager, Gradle with the Android Gradle Plugin, Maven, npm and Vite. Each has its own build commands, its own errors, and its own pitfalls. An agent that has to keep all four environments in mind at once starts confusing the commands and error formats of different platforms and spends extra turns on it.

So I split the agents by environment rather than by layer: each project has its own agent that knows only its platform, its build command, and its directory. The shared module defines the contract. Its public API is exposed to each application in a platform-specific form: Android through an AAR and Desktop through a JAR published to mavenLocal, iOS through the generated Objective-C header, and Web through the exported JavaScript facade and TypeScript declarations (.d.ts). The expect/actual mechanism remains an internal implementation detail of shared.

This defines the role of the orchestrator. It is not a dispatcher that hands out arbitrary tasks, but the component that propagates a contract change: first shared changes, then the new build is distributed to the platforms, and then each platform agent brings the change into its application. Responsibility for decisions is distributed as follows: the orchestrator defines the expected outcome; the shared agent decides what goes into the shared code and how it is exported; the platform agent decides how to implement it in its project, and only that agent can change anything there.

The Harness: Who Does the Work

Everything that controls the agents lives in a separate repository, which I call the harness. The five projects are placed inside its directory, but each of them remains a separate repository on GitHub.

kmp-agents/
├── CLAUDE.md                 shared context for all agents
├── .claude/
│   ├── agents/               definitions of the six agents
│   └── skills/               rules for each platform
├── scripts/
│   ├── propagate.sh          distribute shared code to the platforms
│   ├── build-all.sh          build and check everything
│   ├── check-propagation.sh  verify that changes reach the apps
│   ├── smoke/                check the behavior of shared
│   ├── hooks/                checks on agent actions
│   ├── usage-report.sh       count token usage
│   └── clone-projects.sh     clone the five projects
├── logs/                     build logs and hook denials
└── KMP_template_*            five projects, each with its own GitHub repo

The team is defined in .claude/agents/: six markdown files, one per agent. The frontmatter specifies the model, the allowed tools, and the hooks, and for the executing agents also the turn limit and the Skill. The orchestrator runs as the main session with claude --agent orchestrator. It can call only its five agents and does not write code itself: it simply has no Edit or Write tools. I assigned the models according to the complexity of the decisions. Opus went to the orchestrator and the shared agent, which are responsible for the contract. I assigned Sonnet to Android and iOS, which involve more platform-specific build and integration details. Haiku works on Desktop and Web, where the task is mostly to display a ready-made function on the screen.

---
name: ios-agent
model: sonnet
tools: Read, Edit, Write, Bash
maxTurns: 40
skills:
  - kmp-ios-rules
hooks:
  PreToolUse:
    - matcher: "Edit|Write|NotebookEdit"
      hooks:
        - type: command
          command: "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/scripts/hooks/guard-paths.sh KMP_template_ios"
    - matcher: "Bash"
      hooks:
        - type: command
          command: "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/scripts/hooks/guard-bash.sh ios"
---

An agent gets its knowledge from two sources. The Skill in .claude/skills/ contains the rules for its platform: the exact build command, where to look for the available shared symbols, and what not to touch. The skills field loads the Skill at startup, before the agent's first action. The root CLAUDE.md provides the overall picture: where each project is, how shared reaches the platforms, and who is responsible for what.

The last element is the return contract. Each executing agent finishes its work not with a narrative of what it did, but with a block in a fixed format. The orchestrator later checks this block against reality:

STATUS: done | partial | failed
FILES_CHANGED: list of paths
VERIFIED_BY: command and result (or "not verified" and why)
CONTRACT: which shared symbols it relies on
RISKS: list
NOT_DONE: what is not done and who it should be handed to

Scripts and Hooks

Agents handle decisions well, but they are less reliable with routine work that must be performed the same way every time. So I moved deterministic operations into scripts, while keeping artifact propagation and full-project verification under the orchestrator’s control. propagate.sh builds shared and distributes the artifacts to the platforms. It publishes the Android and JVM artifacts to mavenLocal and updates the XCFramework for iOS, while Web receives the fresh JS build through a symbolic link. In addition, the script downloads missing Maven dependencies for Desktop and checks that the JS dependencies of shared are declared in the web project's package.json. build-all.sh builds all five projects, runs the checks, and prints an "ok / FAIL" table.

An agent may treat a successful build as proof that the task is complete. That makes it essential to ensure that the build actually uses the latest artifacts. The very first check of the delivery chain showed that this was not the case. It turned out that iOS had been building against an XCFramework copied in manually about a year earlier, and Web against an old installation in node_modules. Both builds were green, but they said nothing about whether the new code had actually arrived.

This led to two more checks. check-propagation.sh is a separate diagnostic that the orchestrator runs only on request: it inserts a unique string into commonMain, looks for it in all the built applications, then reverts the change and makes sure the string is gone. The smoke tests in smoke/ call shared and check the returned values: for Desktop through the JVM, and for Web in Node.js, including a simulated browser environment. Android runs unit tests in build-all.sh, while iOS is currently only built. The very first smoke test found a bug that both the build and the diff review had missed: the JS part of shared accessed navigator.userAgent without a check, so outside the browser, for example in Node, the code failed on the first call.

hooks/ contains PreToolUse hooks. They enforce stricter restrictions than prompt instructions, because file changes and command execution are checked by code before they run. Before every Edit or Write, the guard-paths.sh hook normalizes the path and checks that the file is inside the agent's directory. Before every Bash command, the guard-bash.sh hook checks that it is a single plain command without pipes or redirects and that it matches the allowlist for that agent. If a call cannot be parsed, it is denied. A denial does not just block the action, it also tells the agent what to do next:

DENIED: <file> is outside the allowed directory ~/kmp-agents/KMP_template_ios.
You may only edit inside ~/kmp-agents/KMP_template_ios. Edits in another project belong to that project's agent
(shared -> shared-agent, ios -> ios-agent); edits to the harness and scripts belong to the orchestrator.
Do not try to work around this: describe the needed edit in the NOT_DONE field of your report and return it to the orchestrator.

When an agent hits a restriction, it does not look for a workaround but returns the task to the orchestrator with a clear description in NOT_DONE. Every denial is written to a log in logs/, and usage-report.sh uses the session transcripts to count how many tokens each agent consumed; I converted them to dollars separately, using API prices. I will come back to the numbers closer to the end.

How the Agents Work Together

To show the whole chain, I will take one real task: “add the OS version to the contract and display it on all four screens.” I gave it to the orchestrator in a single sentence, and from there it drove the work on its own. First, the orchestrator decided that the contract was changing, which meant the shared agent was needed. On tasks that affected only the platforms, it skipped both the shared agent and propagate.sh and went straight to the platform agents.

The key decisions in this task were made by the shared agent. The question of what goes into shared and how it is exported cannot be hardcoded in rules, which is why I assigned the strongest model to this role. In the browser, the agent detected the OS from the user agent and checked iOS and Android before macOS and Linux, because their user agent strings also contain “Mac OS X” and “Linux”. It deliberately avoided the Node os module, which would have broken the browser build. However, the exact version cannot be obtained from the user agent, because modern browsers freeze it. For example, Chrome and Safari on macOS report a fixed value of 10.15.7, and this is exactly what the web version displays. The agent verified that the new API was available not by the fact that the build succeeded, but through the generated Objective-C header for Swift and the .d.ts for JavaScript, that is, through the interfaces the platform applications will see.

Next, the orchestrator ran propagate.sh and then launched the four platform agents in parallel, in a single call. They did not reimplement the OS detection logic: they checked the exported API, imported the ready-made function from shared, and added a call to it in their UI. As the last step, the orchestrator ran build-all.sh with the smoke tests and checked every report against reality: FILES_CHANGED against git diff, VERIFIED_BY against the full build, and CONTRACT against the actual API. In one of the runs, it noticed an incorrect item in an agent's RISKS and explained what was wrong with it. In another, after a failed build, it identified on its own whose area the failure belonged to and returned the task to the right agent. A commit is made only on a green build.

The value of these rules became clear in another task: updating a shared dependency. After the update, Desktop failed: the new transitive dependency was missing from the local Maven cache, Maven was running offline according to my own rules, and no role had permission to download it. The orchestrator did not look for a workaround: it stopped, committed nothing, identified the cause from the log, and proposed options. Once I added dependency resolution to propagate.sh, the workflow reached a green build without any further manual changes to the application code. The agents did not work around the restrictions but turned them into clear messages about what was missing, and this is exactly the behavior the restrictions were designed for.

What I Learned

Almost every lesson here came from a real failure. Three of them have already appeared above, and in my opinion they apply to any project with multiple agents. First, an agent’s report is a claim, not proof. One of the agents confidently described behavior that did not exist in the code, and only running the code caught it. Second, trustworthy verification has to be in place before the agents, because an agent will honestly report the success of a build that was compiled against a stale artifact. Third, every step of the chain needs an owner. Permissions should be checked not by role but by step: walk through the chain from start to finish and, for each step, ask who is able to perform it.

Two more lessons concern Claude Code itself. A hook of the main session also applies to its subagents. The orchestrator is launched with --agent, so the hooks from its frontmatter became hooks of the whole session and fired inside the subagents as well. All matching hooks run, and a denial from any one of them is enough to block the call. As a result, the platform agents suddenly stopped being able to build their own projects: their commands were also being checked by the orchestrator's hook. The solution is to let the orchestrator's hook pass calls whose input contains the agent_id and agent_type of one of the known agents.

The second lesson: rules that are needed from the very first step should live in a Skill, not in a nested CLAUDE.md. The root CLAUDE.md is loaded at startup, but a nested one is loaded lazily, only after the agent reads some file in that directory. An agent that starts with a build works without its rules. Skills are normally loaded on demand as well, but the skills field in a subagent definition injects their full content before the agent’s first action.

A separate note on cost. Running the OS version task through the orchestrator and five subagents had an estimated API cost of about $1.32, and roughly three quarters of that went to the orchestrator: it makes dozens of calls and re-reads the growing context on each one, which adds up to about 1.2 million cache-read tokens per run. The Haiku agents cost fractions of a cent and handled their part of the work, although I did not compare the same task across different models. The shared agent on Opus was the most expensive of the executing agents, but it was the one making decisions about the contract, and this is not where I would try to save.

Conclusion

For me, the main result of this experiment is that the reliability of an agent team depends less on the models than on what is built around them. KMP turned out to be a convenient basis for such a team: its structure, one contract and four platform-specific environments, itself suggests how to split the work. But the result came not from the agents alone, but from a combination of three things: trustworthy verification, scripts for everything deterministic, and hooks that check agent actions with code rather than with the prompt.

The approach has its limitations. The agents build the projects and call shared, but they do not launch the application windows, so I checked the layouts manually using screenshots. Hooks are a restriction mechanism, not a sandbox: they prevent writing outside the allowed directory, but they do not isolate the process. The conclusions about models and cost are based on a few tasks, so they are a guideline rather than a benchmark. Everything was tested with Claude Code v2.1.296 on macOS, and some of the described behavior, such as the loading of nested CLAUDE.md files, may change in future versions.

The complete harness, including the agents, Skills, hooks, and scripts, is available in the KMP_template_agents repository, and the five projects it works with are in the same GitHub profile. In the next articles, I plan to implement the same architecture in two other ways: in code with the Claude Agent SDK, and through a custom MCP server instead of Bash.

Thanks for your reading. You can also find me on LinkedIn and GitHub.

item.title: CSS @scope Just Reached Every Major Browser.
item.content:encoded:
CSS @scope Just Reached Every Major Browser. Most Developers Are Still Writing BEM Class Names to Do Its Job.

You wrote this rule once and never thought about it again:

/* Looks harmless. Ships. */
.card h2 {
 font-size: 1.25rem;
 margin: 0 0 0.5rem;
}

Three weeks later, someone drops a promo block into a card’s content area. It has its own `<h2>`. It’s now 1.25rem with a bottom margin it was never supposed to have, and nobody can say why, because the promo component doesn’t have a single `.card` class on it. The rule reached through the card, past the boundary you assumed was there, and grabbed it.

So you did what everyone does. You stopped trusting element selectors and wrote `.card__title`, `.card__meta`, `.card — featured .card__title`. You made the class names long enough that collisions became unlikely. That’s BEM, and it works, but notice what it really is: a naming convention standing in for a feature CSS didn’t have.

CSS has it now. And as of the end of last year, it’s in all three major engines.

Here’s what actually changed

`@scope` lets you say where a block of rules is allowed to match. You give it a root, and everything inside only applies to elements within that root’s subtree:

@scope (.card) {
 /* Only matches h2 elements inside a .card, no class on the h2 needed */
 h2 {
 font-size: 1.25rem;
 margin: 0 0 0.5rem;
 }
}

Inside the block, selectors are relative to the root, so `h2` behaves like `:scope h2`. There are a few more pieces:

- `:scope` refers to the root element itself (the `.card`)
- `to (…)` adds a lower boundary, called the scope limit, where matching stops
- inside the block, `&` can stand in for the root as well
- a `<style>` element can use `@scope` with no selector at all, and it scopes to its parent

Chrome and Edge have supported it since version 118. Firefox 146 landed support at the very end of 2025, which completed the set, and it now carries the Baseline “newly available” tag.

The old way vs. the new way

Here’s the BEM version of a card:

<article class="card card - featured">
 <h2 class="card__title">Release notes</h2>
 <p class="card__meta">Updated today</p>
</article>
.card { padding: 1rem; border: 1px solid #e2e8f0; border-radius: 8px; }
.card__title { font-size: 1.25rem; margin: 0 0 0.5rem; }
.card__meta { color: #64748b; }
.card - featured .card__title { color: #b45309; }

And the scoped version:

<article class="card featured">
 <h2>Release notes</h2>
 <p class="meta">Updated today</p>
</article>
@scope (.card) {
 :scope {
 padding: 1rem;
 border: 1px solid #e2e8f0;
 border-radius: 8px;
 }
h2 { font-size: 1.25rem; margin: 0 0 0.5rem; }
 .meta { color: #64748b; }
/* :scope can be combined with a class on the root itself */
 :scope.featured h2 { color: #b45309; }
}

Short class names like `.meta` are fine here because they can only match inside a `.card`. Another component can have its own `.meta` and the two never meet. The markup is cleaner too: bare elements stop needing a class just to be addressable.

One detail matters for anyone worried about specificity. Selectors inside the block don’t pick up extra weight from the root, so `h2` inside `@scope (.card)` is still a plain element selector, specificity-wise. You’re limiting reach, not escalating a fight.

Four things you can actually use this for

1. Component styles that don’t leak

This is the card example above, and it’s the baseline use. Scope each component to its root class and write the inside in plain element and short-class selectors. No naming convention to police in code review.

2. Donut scope: stop before the slotted content

The leak from the opening is exactly what the lower boundary fixes:

<article class="card">
 <h2>Release notes</h2>
 <div class="card-slot">
 <section class="promo">
 <h2>Sponsored</h2>
 </section>
 </div>
</article>
/* Style the card's own h2, but stop at the slot.
 Anything inside .card-slot is outside this scope entirely */
@scope (.card) to (.card-slot) {
 h2 {
 font-size: 1.25rem;
 margin: 0 0 0.5rem;
 }
}

The `<h2>` inside `.promo` is untouched. The shape of the area that matches, from the root down to the limit, is why it’s called a donut scope. This is the case BEM can’t express with naming alone: you’d have to remember to reset every promo element, or rename everything.

Two details are worth knowing before you rely on it. By default the root is inclusive and the limit is exclusive, so the `.card` itself can be matched by `:scope`, while the `.card-slot` and everything under it cannot. And the limit can be made relative to the root with `:scope`, which stops a stray class elsewhere on the page from acting as a boundary:

/* Only a .content that is a direct child of the root counts as the limit.
 A .content nested deeper inside doesn't end the scope */
@scope (.media-object) to (:scope > .content) {
 img { border-radius: 6px; }
}

That precision is what makes the donut safe to use on components that nest inside each other.

3. Nested themes without a source-order fight

Say you have light and dark sections that can nest inside each other, each coloring links:

@scope (.light) {
 a { color: #1e293b; }
}
@scope (.dark) {
 a { color: #f8fafc; }
}
<div class="dark">
 <section class="light">
 <! - Closest root is .light, so this link is dark slate,
 even though the .dark rule appears later in the file →
 <a href="/docs">Read the docs</a>
 </section>
</div>

`@scope` adds a cascade step called scoping proximity: when two scoped rules tie on specificity, the one whose root is fewer levels above the element wins, and that beats source order. Importance, cascade layers and specificity still come first. Before this, nested theming meant either deep selector chains or a custom property on every wrapper.

4. One-off styles right next to the markup

Inside a `<style>` element, `@scope` with no selector scopes to the element’s parent:

<section class="pricing">
 <style>
 @scope {
 h3 { letter-spacing: 0.02em; }
 .price { font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }
 }
 </style>
<h3>Pro</h3>
 <p class="price">$12</p>
</section>

This is useful for a CMS block, a blog post or a template where you can’t touch the global stylesheet but still don’t want your rules escaping. The cost is that the CSS ships again with every instance of the component you render.

The honest limitations

It limits selectors, not styles. This is the one people misread. `@scope` constrains what a selector can match. It doesn’t isolate styles: inherited properties like `color` and `font-family` still flow down into the donut hole. If your card sets a color and the promo doesn’t, the promo inherits it. CSS Modules gives you hashed class names; `@scope` does not give you that kind of isolation.

Class names are still global. Your `.card` root is still a global class. Two unrelated components that both use `.card` as their root will both scope to it. You’ve removed the need for long inner names, not the need to name roots sensibly.

You can’t reach outside the subtree. A selector like `:scope + p` inside a scope is invalid, because it would match an element outside the root. Sibling-of-root styling still lives outside `@scope`.

`&` is the shaky part. MDN specifically warns that `&` inside `@scope` is handled differently across engines and versions. Stick to `:scope` for the root until you’ve tested the exact patterns you plan to ship.

Outside `@scope`, `:scope` means `:root`. Fine in stylesheets, but it will surprise you if you paste a scoped rule out of its block.

In JavaScript, use `:scope` for relative selectors. `querySelectorAll(“> div”)` doesn’t work. `querySelectorAll(“:scope > div”)` does.

The inline `<style>` pattern repeats. Reuse that component fifty times and the CSS is emitted fifty times.

How to think about this right now

You don’t need to rewrite a working BEM codebase. If a stylesheet is stable, leave it.

For new components, `@scope (.component)` is a better default than inventing a naming scheme. You write simpler selectors, the markup has fewer classes, and the leak from the top of this article can’t happen.

Reach for the donut scope the moment a component accepts slotted content or user-generated content. That’s where scoping bugs actually show up, and where naming conventions have never helped.

Keep your existing tool when you need what it provides. If CSS Modules is giving you hashed names and a build-time guarantee, `@scope` doesn’t replace that. It replaces the part where you were typing `card__title` by hand to avoid a collision.

The sources I checked are careful to say `@scope` reduces the need for complex selectors rather than replacing BEM outright, and that’s the right read. But “I’d rather not write BEM for new work” is now a legitimate position backed by all three browsers.

CSS @scope Just Reached Every Major Browser. was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
